item.title: Writing a paper, level by level
item.description:
Each level of a paper holds one thing. A paper carries one message, a section does one job, a paragraph develops one idea, and a sentence adds one new point. Plan and revise from the outside in: a perfect sentence inside a paragraph you later cut is wasted effort.

Paper 1 message
Section 1 job
Paragraph 1 idea
Sentence 1 new point
Word 1 term per concept

The same pattern repeats at every scale: context, then content, then conclusion. Every rule below carries a label for how strong its evidence is: Experimental Correlational Descriptive Expert. They are explained at the end.

The workflow

  1. Message. Make the figures, then write the take-home message in one or two sentences. Leave it a day, then revise it.
  2. Skeleton. Put the figures in order. Draft the five pivotal paragraphs first (see Section), then one topic sentence for every other paragraph.
  3. Draft. Write fast and do not polish. A common order is Methods, Results, Discussion, Introduction, Abstract, Title.
  4. Revise from the top down. Paper, sections, paragraphs, sentences, words.
  5. Test with a reader. Someone outside your subfield restates the message in their own words.

To plan before drafting, the paper brief turns stages 1 and 2 into a list of questions.

Paper

Goal: the reader finishes with one message they can repeat.

Write

  1. Write the take-home message in one sentence: what the result changes, not only what you found.
  2. Write the story as And, But, Therefore.
  3. Choose the three to five figures that carry the message and order them as an argument.
  4. Keep hypotheses, predictions, analyses, results and discussion points in the same order everywhere.
  5. Write a working title that states the finding, not the topic.

Check

  • Can a colleague restate the message after reading only the abstract?
  • Does every section serve the message? What does not goes to the supplement or out.
  • If the Introduction lists three predictions, do Methods, Results and Discussion follow the same three, in the same order?
  • Is any conclusion stronger than the results support?

Example (invented, on a mountain pine beetle forecasting topic)

And mountain pine beetle outbreaks have killed pine over large areas of western Canada, and managers must decide where to act a year in advance. But most outbreak maps describe where beetles are now, not where they will spread next. Therefore we built a model that forecasts spread one year ahead and tested it against past outbreak records.

A result

Beetle spread was lower after winters with colder minimum temperatures.

A take-home message

Forecasts of next year’s spread should weight winter minimum temperature more than current models do.

A result says what you found; a take-home message says what it changes. The same goes for titles: “Investigating the dynamics of beetle spread using a forecasting framework” names a topic, while “Cold winters slow beetle spread the following year” states a finding. Use the second kind only when your results support it.

Evidence: Expert for the steps (Fahrig; Magnusson 1996; Mensh and Kording 2017; Olson 2015). Correlational more narrative abstracts and short, result-stating titles are cited more (Hillier et al. 2016; Paiva et al. 2012). Experimental result-stating titles did not change how strongly readers believed the findings (Research Integrity and Peer Review, 2016), so they help readers find a paper rather than persuade them.

Section

Goal: each section does one job, and together they form an hourglass.

Section Its job
Abstract The whole story in small: context, gap, approach, main result with numbers, implication.
Introduction From the broad problem, to what is known, to the gap, ending with the aim of this paper.
Methods Enough to reproduce the work, in the same order as the Results.
Results One finding per paragraph. Each paragraph opens with the finding, not the method.
Discussion The answer first, then how it fits current knowledge, limitations, and implications.

The numbered pins are the five pivotal paragraphs (McGill 2016): (1) the big question, (2) this paper’s question, (3) the main answer, (4) back to the big question, and (5) the abstract. Draft them first; the rest fills in between.

Check

  • Read only the first sentence of each paragraph. Do they tell the story alone?
  • Does the Introduction end on exactly the question the Discussion answers, stated without methods?
  • Are the limitations in the middle of the Discussion? The first and last paragraphs carry the emphasis.
  • Does the Discussion add meaning, or repeat the Results?

Opens with the method

We fitted a generalized additive model with winter minimum temperature as a predictor of spread.

Opens with the finding

Beetles spread less after colder winters (Fig. 2). We tested this with a generalized additive model…

Evidence: Expert for structure (McGill 2016; Mensh and Kording 2017; Heard 2016). Experimental headings improve readers’ memory of a text’s topic structure (Lorch et al. 2013).

Paragraph

Goal: one idea, stated first, then developed, with each sentence linked to the one before.

Part What it does
Link (optional) A few words tying this paragraph to the last: “In contrast”, “This pattern”.
Topic sentence The paragraph’s point, stated as a claim. Skimming first sentences should give the argument.
Support, 3–4 sentences Evidence, reasoning, citations, figure references. Each opens with something the reader already has.
Close (optional) What the point means, or a hand-off to the next paragraph. Not a summary.

In the 148 research papers I measured from my own reading library, a typical paragraph ran about 160 words and five to six sentences.

Example (invented numbers). Shading marks information the reader already has and what each sentence adds:

Forecasts of beetle spread need an accurate map of current infestations. These maps come mainly from annual aerial surveys. Aerial surveys, however, record trees attacked the previous year, so every forecast starts one year behind the outbreak.

Each sentence picks up what the previous one ended on, then adds one new thing at its end.

Check

  • Can you sum up the paragraph in one line? If you need two, split it.
  • Do the sentence subjects form a chain the reader can follow?
  • Do transitions show logic (because, however, therefore) rather than just add (moreover, additionally)?
  • Who reads this paragraph? In the abstract and introduction, state every link; in technical methods, specialists can fill small gaps.

Evidence: Experimental putting known information before new speeds comprehension (Haviland and Clark 1974), and how much to spell out depends on the reader’s background (McNamara et al. 1996). Expert for topic sentences (Fahrig; Heard 2016).

Sentence

Goal: the reader understands the sentence on the first read.

Position What goes there
Start (topic position) Old information: who or what the sentence is about.
Subject and verb The character and its action, early and close together.
End (stress position) The new, important point. Readers weight it most.

Write

  1. Find the main character and the action.
  2. Make them the subject and verb, close together, near the start.
  3. Put the new, important information at the end.
  4. Split the sentence if it carries more than one new idea.
  5. For a result, state its direction and size, not just that groups differed.

Before

An analysis of the relationship between winter minimum temperature and the survival of overwintering larvae was performed.

After

We tested whether colder winters reduced the survival of overwintering larvae.

Before

Stand age was the strongest predictor of attack, according to our model.

After

In our model, the strongest predictor of attack was stand age.

Before

Attack rates differed between young and mature stands (Table 1).

After

Mature stands were attacked about twice as often as young stands (Table 1).

Evidence: Experimental readers recalled important ideas better when actions were verbs rather than nouns (Spyridakis and Isakson 1998) and misread passive sentences more often than active ones (Ferreira 2003). Experimental keeping linked words close lowers processing cost in controlled sentences (Gibson 1998), but in natural reading the effect appeared only at nouns (Demberg and Keller 2008): mixed. Expert for stress position (Gopen and Swan 1990; Williams and Bizup).

Word

Goal: each word is precise, simple, and used the same way throughout.

  1. Choose one term per concept and keep it. Keep a term list for the paper.
  2. Cut jargon and acronyms where you can; define the rest at first use.
  3. Prefer concrete words: organisms, places, numbers, processes.
  4. Match hedges to the strength of the evidence.
  5. Cut filler.
Instead of Write Why
utilize use Same meaning, shorter.
in order to to Filler.
it is important to note that (cut) If it matters, the sentence shows it.
may potentially suggest may suggest One hedge, matched to the evidence. Do not cut the last one.
outbreak … epidemic … infestation outbreak, every time Synonyms make readers think you mean different things.
spatiotemporal dynamics where and when beetles spread Concrete over abstract.

Evidence: Experimental needlessly complex words lowered readers’ opinion of the writer (Oppenheimer 2006); jargon lowered processing fluency even when definitions were given (Bullock et al. 2019); hedged news stories made scientists seem more trustworthy to lay readers (Jensen 2008). Correlational more jargon in titles and abstracts went with fewer citations (Martínez and Mammola 2021). Descriptive 79% of acronyms in the literature are used fewer than ten times (Barnett and Doubleday 2020).

How big is each part?

Count the jobs first, then check the length. The sizes below are what is typical in the papers I read, not targets.

Introduction~1,000 words · 18%5–7 paragraphs
Methods~1,600 words · 30%7–15 paragraphs
Results~900 words · 18%5–10 paragraphs
Discussion~1,600 words · 30%7–12 paragraphs

Widths show each section’s median share of the text; each small box is one paragraph at the median; ranges are the middle half of papers. Descriptive

  1. Count the jobs. One paragraph per question, prediction, analysis or finding.
  2. Check the budget. Paragraphs ≈ section words ÷ 160.
  3. Check each paragraph. Over about 250 words, it probably holds two ideas. Under about 60 words, merge it or develop it.
Section Paragraph slots, in order
Introduction Big question (1) · what is known (2–4) · the gap (1) · question and numbered predictions (1)
Methods Overview · one per data source · one per model or measurement · one per analysis, in prediction order · software and code
Results Optional data overview · one or two per finding, finding first, in prediction order
Discussion The answer · one or two per finding · limitations (in the middle) · implications · back to the big question

A methods paper has different slots; the paper brief gives both versions.

Where these numbers come from. A script read the PDFs in my Zotero library, found the four section headings, and split each section into paragraphs from the page layout. It kept 148 research papers, mostly in forest insect ecology. Tables and captions were left out, so Results look shorter than they are, and the Discussion includes any Conclusions section.

Median (middle half of papers), n = 148.
Section Words Paragraphs Words per paragraph
Introduction 998 (805–1,159) 6 (5–7) 160 (135–183)
Methods 1,606 (1,047–2,298) 10 (7–15) 157 (134–185)
Results 926 (650–1,442) 7 (5–10) 146 (118–170)
Discussion 1,608 (1,224–2,114) 9 (7–12) 173 (142–196)

The practice loop

Guides describe good writing; getting better at it takes practice. Work on one skill at a time, with quick feedback and repetition (Kellogg 2008).

  1. Pick one skill from your recurring problems: stress position, topic sentences, hidden verbs.
  2. Study a model: a short passage from a well-written paper that does it well, with what it does named.
  3. Rewrite a passage of your own applying that one skill.
  4. Get quick feedback on that skill only, then do one more round.
  5. Log the pattern in a personal style guide when a habit is fixed or keeps returning.

Evidence: studying models and sentence combining both improved writing in a meta-analysis of school students, so their transfer to research writing is assumed (Graham and Perin 2007). Peer feedback improved writing quality across 60 studies (Wei and Liu 2024). No schedule is prescribed: writing every day is not shown to beat other routines (Sword 2016).

How strong is this advice?

Label Meaning Example
Experimental Tested by changing a text and measuring readers. Most tests used short texts and student or lay readers. More accessible abstracts improved readers’ understanding and confidence (Freeling et al. 2021).
Correlational Links between writing features and citations. They show associations, not causes. More narrative abstracts were cited more (Hillier et al. 2016).
Descriptive Trends in the literature. Abstracts have become harder to read since 1881 (Plavén-Sigray et al. 2017).
Expert Advice from experienced writers and editors. It rests on how readers process text but is untested. Most of the structure above.

Readability formulas, which count word and sentence length, are not a measure of clarity: in 4,191 forestry abstracts they showed no link with citations (Jiang et al. 2026). Use sentence length only as a warning sign.

Sources

Guides. Gopen GD, Swan JA (1990) The science of scientific writing. American Scientist. · Heard SB (2016) The Scientist’s Guide to Writing. Princeton University Press. · Magnusson WE (1996) How to write backwards. Bulletin of the Ecological Society of America 77:88. · McGill B (2016) The 5 pivotal paragraphs in a paper. Dynamic Ecology. · Mensh B, Kording K (2017) Ten simple rules for structuring papers. PLOS Computational Biology. · Olson R (2015) Houston, We Have a Narrative. University of Chicago Press. · Williams JM, Bizup J. Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace. · Fahrig L. How to write a scientific paper that people will want to read (and cite!), workshop slides.

Research.

  • Freeling B (now Ryba R) et al. (2021) Better writing in scientific publications builds reader confidence and understanding. Frontiers in Psychology 12:714321.
  • Gibson E (1998) Linguistic complexity: locality of syntactic dependencies. Cognition 68:1–76.

  • Jensen JD (2008) Scientific uncertainty in news coverage of cancer research: effects of hedging on scientists’ and journalists’ credibility. Human Communication Research. doi:10.1111/j.1468-2958.2008.00324.x

item.title: Start writing: the paper brief
item.description:
A blank page is hard; a list of questions is not. This brief asks the questions a paper has to answer, in an order that builds the outline as you go. Each answer feeds a specific paragraph, so a finished brief is a finished skeleton.

Download the brief to fill in: Word (.docx) · Markdown (.md)

How to use it:

  1. Choose the paper type (Step 0).
  2. Answer Blocks A to D in writing, in order.
  3. Pass the four gates.
  4. Turn each slot into a topic sentence, then draft paragraph by paragraph, using the level-by-level method.

Step 0: choose the paper type

Decide this first, because six of the questions change with the type. A regular paper answers a question about nature; a methods paper offers a way of doing something that others can reuse.

Regular paper Methods paper
Take-home message is about The system: species, forests, outbreaks The procedure: how to compare, measure, forecast
Introduction ends on A question and numbered predictions A gap in existing methods, independent of any study system
Core of the paper Results that answer the predictions The method, then its evaluation
Evidence Data from the study system Simulations across a range of conditions, comparison with alternatives, error rates
Case study Is the paper One short worked example, often a single figure
Discussion What the finding means for ecology or management When to use the method, its limits, how to implement it

Test 1. Draft the take-home message roughly. If its subject is the system, it is a regular paper; if its subject is a procedure, it is a methods paper.

Test 2. Would the paper still matter if the case study were a different species or region? If yes, it leans methods. A good methods paper is about the method, not the study system (Ellison 2023).

If a project holds both a new method and a new finding, two papers are often clearer than one. Methods journals also set the format: at Methods in Ecology and Evolution, a Research Article (a new general method) and a Workflow (a new pipeline of existing procedures) run to 8,000 words, and an Application or Practical Tool to 4,000.

Writing backwards: what it gains, what it costs

The brief starts from your results and works back to the question, following Magnusson’s “write backwards” method: conclusions first, then only the results, methods, discussion and introduction they need. It is worth using, but only with safeguards, because its main risk is quietly rewriting the question to fit the answer.

What happens Evidence
Gain: content before style The story is fixed first; style is easier to correct afterwards. Expert
Gain: report what matters You stop reporting every analysis in the order you ran it (Heard 2016). Expert
Gain: planning improves the text Outlining before drafting produced better documents than not outlining (Kellogg 1988). Experimental
Gain: an easier start You begin from what you know best: your results and figures. Expert
Cost: HARKing Writing the Introduction last invites presenting an unexpected finding as if it had been predicted (Kerr 1998). 51% of 807 ecologists and evolutionary biologists admitted doing so at least once (Fraser et al. 2018). Survey
Cost: selective reporting “Only the results the conclusions need” can slide into dropping inconvenient ones. 64% admitted not reporting non-significant results (Fraser et al. 2018). Survey
Cost: overselling Conclusion-first framing can push claims past the evidence. Expert
Cost: locking in too early Outlining improves text quality but can stop the new ideas that come from drafting, at least for some writers (Galbraith and Baaijen 2018). Experimental, early

The brief keeps the gains and blocks the costs with five safeguards:

  1. Record the original question first. Question C1 asks what you set out to test before you saw the results. Anything not in it is reported as exploratory.
  2. List the results that do not fit. Question B3 has a line for them; they stay in the paper.
  3. Calibrate claims. Each conclusion carries the hedge its evidence needs.
  4. Leave room to discover. If you cannot answer B1 yet, write a rough discussion freely first, outline what you wrote, then return to the brief.
  5. Change the plan for a reason. Revise the brief when a better story appears, but only if you can say why it is better (Heard 2016).

Block A: reader and venue

# Question Feeds
A1 Who is the reader? Name one real person outside your subfield who should understand the paper. How much each section spells out
A2 Target journal, article type and word limit. Paragraph budget = words ÷ 160. Paragraph count per section
A3 Regular or methods paper (Step 0)? One line on why. Which template and question versions

How much to spell out depends on what the reader already knows (McNamara et al. 1996), and experts misjudge what novices find hard (Hinds 1999). A named reader makes both concrete. Experimental

Block B: the answer first

# Question Feeds
B1 Your conclusions: at most five, one sentence each, no “however”. Methods paper: what the method does better than existing ones, with numbers. Discussion ¶1; abstract
B2 Your figures (about five at most) and tables (about four), in the order that best tells the story. One line each: what should the reader see? Results, one or two ¶ per figure
B3 The results each conclusion needs, with direction, size and figure. Then, separately: results that do not fit the conclusions. Methods paper: performance results (accuracy, error rates, sensitivity) and the comparison with alternatives. Results ¶; Discussion limitations
B4 The take-home message in one sentence: not what you found, but what it changes. Leave it a day, then revise. Last sentence of the abstract; Discussion ¶1; title
B5 The central question and its answer, in two sentences. Introduction last ¶; Discussion ¶1

From Magnusson (conclusions, then only the results they need), Heard (figure shuffling and the two-sentence mini-summary) and Fahrig (the take-home message as an implication). Expert

Block C: the question and the argument

Answer C1 from your notes or proposal, not from memory of the results.

# Question Feeds
C1 The original question and predictions, as they stood before you saw the results. Mark any that changed, and any new ones: those are reported as exploratory. Methods paper: the performance claims you set out to test. Introduction last ¶; the order of everything after it
C2 Numbered predictions, P1, P2…, in the order the paper will answer them. Introduction last ¶; Methods, Results and Discussion order
C3 The big question your field cares about, and your pitch: resolves a controversy · a gap that blocks a wider goal · blocks a practical problem · a model system for a wider field · a new path to a hard goal. Methods paper: the task researchers need to do, in any system. Introduction ¶1; Discussion last ¶
C4 What the reader must know first: two to four points, each with its key references. Methods paper: how the task is done now, and where that falls short. Introduction ¶2–4
C5 The gap and why it matters, without “no studies have” or “to increase our understanding”. Methods paper: the gap in methods, stated without your study system. Introduction gap ¶
C6 For each prediction: the data and analysis needed, and only those. Methods paper: the method’s components and assumptions, the simulation design, the alternatives compared, the case study. Methods ¶, in prediction order
C7 The story in three lines: And (context), But (gap), Therefore (what you did and found). Abstract; Introduction arc

From Heard (the story summary and the five pitches), Fahrig (flow-through order), McGill (the pivotal first paragraph), Olson (And, But, Therefore) and Ellison (methods papers). Expert

Block D: meaning and limits

# Question Feeds
D1 For each conclusion: does it agree with, extend or contradict earlier work? Name the papers. Discussion ¶2–5, in prediction order
D2 The limitations that could change a conclusion, and by how much. Methods paper: the method’s assumptions, and when someone should not use it. Discussion middle, never first or last
D3 What changes for management or theory? Methods paper: how to implement it; where the code and data are. Discussion implications ¶
D4 A working title that states the finding: short, no question mark. Methods paper: a title that says what the method does. Title
D5 What you are leaving out, and why: not relevant, redundant, or a separate paper. Conflicting results never go here. Supplement or another paper

Four gates before drafting

  • Message. B4 is one sentence, states an implication, and passes the Step 0 test. You left it a day and revised it. Your reader from A1 could repeat it.
  • Honesty. C1 came from your notes, not your results. Every prediction not in C1 is labelled exploratory. B3 lists the results that do not fit, and D5 hides none of them.
  • Order. The predictions in C2, figures in B2, analyses in C6 and comparisons in D1 all follow the same order.
  • Budget. The paragraph count from the tables below fits the A2 budget. If it is over, cut a prediction or move it to the supplement before writing.

Where each answer goes

When the gates pass, write one topic sentence per slot from its answers. That list is your skeleton. Then draft each paragraph as link, topic sentence, three or four supporting sentences, and close.

Regular paper. Typical paragraph counts are from 148 papers I measured.

Section Paragraph slot Built from
Introduction (5–7 ¶) Big question C3
What the reader must know (2–4 ¶) C4
The gap C5
Question and numbered predictions C1, C2, B5
Methods (7–15 ¶) Overview C6, C7
Data, then one ¶ per model or measurement, then one per analysis C6, in C2 order
Results (5–10 ¶) One or two ¶ per finding, finding first B2, B3, in C2 order
Discussion (7–12 ¶) The answer B1, B4, B5
One or two ¶ per finding D1
Limitations, in the middle D2, B3
Implications D3
Back to the big question C3, B4
Abstract and title Context, gap, approach, result, implication C7, B3, B4, D4

Methods paper. Sizes are not measured; use the journal’s limit (A2).

Section Paragraph slot Built from
Introduction The task researchers need to do C3
How it is done now, and where that falls short C4
The gap in methods C5
What the new method does B4, C1
Method Overview, then one ¶ per component, assumptions stated C6
Evaluation Simulation design C6
One ¶ per performance result; comparison with alternatives B2, B3
Case study One or two ¶, often one figure B2, C6
Discussion What the method does better B1, D1
When to use it, and when not, in the middle D2
Implementation, code and data D3
Back to the task C3, B4

Sources

Guides. Fahrig L. How to write a scientific paper that people will want to read (and cite!), workshop slides. · Heard SB (2016) The Scientist’s Guide to Writing, ch. 7 and 16. Princeton University Press. · Magnusson WE (1996) How to write backwards. Bulletin of the Ecological Society of America 77:88. · McGill B (2016) The 5 pivotal paragraphs in a paper. Dynamic Ecology. · Olson R (2015) Houston, We Have a Narrative.

Research and journal policy.

  • Fraser H, Parker T, Nakagawa S, Barnett A, Fidler F (2018) Questionable research practices in ecology and evolution. PLOS ONE 13:e0200303.
  • Galbraith D, Baaijen VM (2018) The work of writing: raiding the inarticulate. Educational Psychologist.
  • Hinds PJ (1999) The curse of expertise: the effects of expertise and debiasing methods on prediction of novice performance. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied.
  • Kellogg RT (1988) Attentional overload and writing performance: effects of rough draft and outline strategies. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 14:355–365.
  • Kerr NL (1998) HARKing: hypothesizing after the results are known. Personality and Social Psychology Review.
  • McNamara DS, Kintsch E, Songer NB, Kintsch W (1996) Are good texts always better? Cognition and Instruction.
